name: Erewhon Beverly Blvd (Fairfax)
who: The chain's original store, a 1968 macrobiotic shop turned ultra-premium celebrity grocery flagship at 7660 Beverly Blvd since 1991.
why: The most photographed, most celebrity-trafficked health food store in the country, credited with inventing the $20 smoothie era.
takeaway: The original celebrity grocery flagship — go for star-spotting and the smoothie bar that started the $20-smoothie era.

name: Erewhon Calabasas
who: The chain's 2014 second-generation location in the Kardashian-adjacent Calabasas foothills, one of Erewhon's largest stores with a spacious hot bar.
why: Independently iconic as a celebrity-spotting destination in its own right, distinct in clientele and layout from the Fairfax original.
takeaway: Erewhon's Kardashian-adjacent outpost — go for the spacious hot bar and celebrity-spotting distinct from the Fairfax original.

name: Whole Foods Market (Austin flagship)
who: The mothership flagship store blocks from the original 1980 North Lamar location where four Austin natural-food retailers launched the entire natural-supermarket format.
why: The store that invented the natural-foods supermarket as a category, surviving a 1981 flood to build what became a $20B+ business.
takeaway: Study it as the birthplace of the natural-foods supermarket format, not for anything unique on the shelves.

name: Lassens Natural Foods & Vitamins (La Brea, LA)
who: California vitamin-and-natural-foods chain founded 1971 in Camarillo by Oda Lassen; the La Brea, LA store is its best-known city outpost, minutes from Erewhon's original.
why: A family-run, three-generation vitamin-shop institution that predates the celebrity-grocer wave by decades.
takeaway: Go for a three-generation family vitamin shop that predates the whole celebrity-grocer wave by decades.

name: Bristol Farms (Rolling Hills Estates original)
who: Upscale Southern California supermarket chain founded 1982 by former wholesale butchers who modeled it on Harrods' food halls; the original store still operates in Rolling Hills Estates.
why: The white-tablecloth end of health-adjacent grocery, long favored by affluent South Bay and Beverly Hills shoppers for its butcher counters and produce theatre.
takeaway: Go for butcher counters and produce theatre modeled on Harrods — the white-tablecloth end of health-adjacent grocery.

name: Lazy Acres Natural Market (Santa Barbara original)
who: Independent organic grocer founded 1991 in Santa Barbara, now a small West Coast banner under the same ownership group (Good Food Holdings) as Bristol Farms and New Seasons.
why: A quieter, neighborhood-scaled organic grocer often named alongside Erewhon and Lassens as an LA-region alternative.
takeaway: Go for a quieter, neighborhood-scaled alternative to Erewhon and Lassens in the LA-region organic-grocery scene.

name: Moon Juice (Melrose Ave, LA)
who: Adaptogen-and-cold-press-juice shop opened 2011 by Amanda Chantal Bacon; the original storefront that launched the 'dust' wellness-supplement category.
why: A tiny shop that became a reference point for the entire US adaptogen and wellness-tonic industry.
takeaway: The tiny original storefront that launched the whole US 'dust' adaptogen-supplement category — go for the cold-press juices.

name: Natural Grocers (Golden/Lakewood, CO origin)
who: Founded 1955 as door-to-door 'Vitamin Cottage' by Margaret and Philip Isely; first storefront opened in Lakewood, CO in 1963, now headquartered nearby in Golden with 165+ US stores.
why: One of the true origin points of the US health-food-store industry, still education-focused after seven decades.
takeaway: Go to see one of the true origin points of the US health-food industry, still education-focused after seven decades.

name: Sprouts Farmers Market (Chandler, AZ original)
who: First Sprouts store, opened 2002 by the Boney family (descendants of a 1943 San Diego produce stand); grew into a 400+ store national chain.
why: Proved a mainstream, no-frills organic-and-bulk format could scale nationally without soda aisles or junk-food end caps.
takeaway: Go to see the first store that proved organic-and-bulk retail could scale nationally without soda-aisle junk food.

name: Jimbo's Naturally (North Park, San Diego original)
who: Organic grocer opened 1984 by Jimbo Someck after leaving a food co-op; the original North Park store anchors a respected six-store San Diego chain now 40+ years old.
why: A San Diego institution known for dropping plastic bags in 2008 and strict local/regenerative-organic sourcing standards.
takeaway: Go for strict regenerative-organic sourcing at the San Diego grocer that dropped plastic bags back in 2008.

name: Mother's Market & Kitchen (Costa Mesa original)
who: Organic grocer-and-kitchen opened 1978 by the MacGurn family with backing from a local yoga center; the original Costa Mesa store anchors an 11-store Southern California chain.
why: One of the longest-running organic grocers in the US, built around a yoga/wellness community rather than as a retail play from day one.
takeaway: Go to see an organic grocer that grew out of a yoga center's community, not a retail plan.

name: Down to Earth Organic and Natural (King St, Honolulu)
who: Hawaii's homegrown organic-and-vegetarian grocer, founded 1977 in Wailuku, Maui; the King Street, Honolulu store opened the same year and remains the flagship after a 2008 renovation.
why: The islands' definitive health-food retailer, running community farmers' markets and free senior meals since its earliest days.
takeaway: Go for the free senior meals and farmers' markets this Hawaii-grown grocer has run since 1977.

name: New Seasons Market (Raleigh Hills, Portland original)
who: Grocery chain founded 1999 by three Portland grocery veterans; the Raleigh Hills store was the first of what grew into roughly 20 Pacific Northwest locations.
why: Defined Portland's local-first, sustainability-first grocery identity a decade before it became a national trend.
takeaway: Go to see the store that defined Portland's local-first grocery identity a decade before it went national.

name: Central Market (North Lamar, Austin original)
who: H-E-B's gourmet/natural-foods banner, opened 1994 on North Lamar in Austin, within blocks of Whole Foods' birthplace; built around scratch bakeries, in-house butchers, and market-style produce.
why: Shows a regional chain can build a genuinely premium, foodie-driven natural-foods format without going fully corporate-national.
takeaway: Go for scratch bakeries and in-house butchers proving a regional chain can go premium without going corporate.
